clinicalPearls: A large (typically over two centimetres) demyelinating brain lesion that mimics a tumour or abscess
It may be the first presentation of multiple sclerosis or occur in established disease
Characteristic MRI features include an incomplete (open) ring of enhancement and relatively little mass effect or oedema for the lesion size
The main concern is distinguishing it from a high-grade glioma, lymphoma or abscess to avoid unnecessary resection
Advanced imaging and, when needed, biopsy help confirm demyelination
It usually responds to corticosteroids, and management otherwise follows that of multiple sclerosis
reference.pathophysiology: Tumefactive multiple sclerosis is a form of inflammatory demyelination in which a large focus of myelin breakdown, perivascular inflammation and reactive astrocytosis forms a mass-like lesion. The active demyelinating edge, where the blood-brain barrier is disrupted, produces the characteristic open-ring enhancement facing the cortex, while the relatively preserved deep margin and modest mass effect reflect the non-neoplastic, inflammatory nature. Recognising these features distinguishes it from neoplasia and infection.
additionalDifferentials: Other inflammatory demyelinating disease (ADEM, neuromyelitis optica)
additionalInvestigations: MRI with contrast, including advanced sequences (perfusion, spectroscopy)
Assessment for dissemination in space and time
Brain biopsy where malignancy or infection cannot be excluded
Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies to exclude mimics
redFlags: Imaging or clinical features favouring malignancy or abscess
Rapid neurological deterioration or raised intracranial pressure
Atypical features suggesting neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
reference.prognosis: Many lesions respond well to corticosteroids with good recovery, and the longer-term course follows that of the underlying demyelinating disease; misdiagnosis as tumour risks harmful surgery.
pitfalls: Resecting the lesion as a presumed tumour
Not recognising the open-ring enhancement pattern
Overlooking neuromyelitis optica or MOG-associated disease
Failing to obtain cerebrospinal fluid and antibody studies
management: High-dose corticosteroids as first-line treatment of the acute tumefactive lesion
Advanced imaging (perfusion, spectroscopy) and, when necessary, biopsy to confirm demyelination and avoid unnecessary neurosurgical resection
Establishment of disease-modifying therapy for the underlying multiple sclerosis once confirmed
Symptomatic management of seizures, spasticity and focal deficits with neurorehabilitation
Review of any disease-modifying drug implicated in triggering the lesion and monitoring of treatment response
Neurology and neuroimmunology referral with structured multiple sclerosis follow-up
